title: Anger and conflict
hook: Someone at the masjid corrects you rudely. Your mom mocks your prayer. Here's what to do in the next ten seconds.

screens.text: Everyone gets angry. Converts get extra chances: family who push your buttons, and sometimes Muslims who forget their manners. Today is a plan for the heat of the moment.
A man asked the Prophet ﷺ for advice. He said: **don't get angry.** The man asked again and again, and got the same answer every time [Bukhari 6116].
bubbles: Feeling anger isn't a sin. Anger can even be right, at injustice [Being Muslim, Spiritual Refinement]. What counts is what you do next.

screens.prompt: The Prophet ﷺ said real strength isn't overpowering people. Who is the strong one?
screens.answer: The one who controls themselves when angry
screens.feedback: That's it [Bukhari 6114]. Self-control is the real strength.

screens.prompt: Anger is rising. Put these steps, drawn from the Prophet's teaching ﷺ, in a sensible order.
items: Say *a'udhu billahi minash-shaytanir-rajim* (I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the outcast)
If you're standing, sit down; if that doesn't help, lie down
Come back later, calm, to deal with the problem
screens.feedback: Seeking refuge [Bukhari 6115], changing position [Abu Dawud 4782], and silence [Bukhari 6018] all come from his teaching.

cards.back: It breaks the spiral and turns you toward Allah [Bukhari 6115].
Changing position cools the body [Abu Dawud 4782].
Silence keeps you from saying what you can't take back: say good or stay quiet [Bukhari 6018].
Stepping away isn't losing. You can always come back to the conversation. You can't un-say a cruel sentence.

screens.situation: After Dhuhr at the masjid, an older man tells Marcus loudly, in front of others: "Brother, your prayer is all wrong. Didn't anyone teach you?" Marcus feels his face go hot.

options.text: Breathe, say "Thanks, I'm still learning," and later ask his mentor to check his prayer
options.feedback: Yes. He keeps his dignity, cools things down, and still gets the correction checked by someone he trusts.
Understandable, but it turns a rude moment into a fight in the masjid. A calm reply ends it faster.

options.text: Never go back to that masjid
options.feedback: Not quite. One rude person isn't the community. Don't let him take the masjid from you.
Not quite. A heated debate in public rarely teaches anyone. Check it later, calmly.

screens.text: **Pardon, without being a doormat.** Allah praises those who hold in their anger and pardon people; He loves those who do good [Q 3:134].
bubbles: Pardoning doesn't mean pretending nothing happened. You can still set a boundary, ask someone to speak to you privately, or tell {{mentor.name}}.
And masjids are full of people still working on themselves. Including you.
Someone's anger involves threats or makes you feel unsafe? That's not for patience: call 911 if you're in danger, and tell {{mentor.name}}.

screens.situation: Destiny's mom, stressed after work, mocks her as she lays out her prayer mat: "There she goes again with her little routine."

options.text: Pray calmly, then later, when things are quiet, tell her gently that it hurt and ask how her day was
options.feedback: Yes. She protects her prayer and her relationship, and raises it when both are calm.

options.text: Fire back about her mom's own habits
options.feedback: Not quite. It wins a moment and starts a war. Answering with something better works far better [Q 41:34].

options.text: Skip the prayer to avoid the comments
options.feedback: Not quite. The prayer is still due. Find a quieter spot or time if you need to, but pray.

screens.prompt: What usually sets you off: a person, a topic, being tired or hungry? Write it down, then pick which of today's tools you'll try first next time.

chips: What if I'm angry at someone at the masjid and can't let it go?
How do I apologize after I lost my temper?
Is it wrong to be angry at injustice?
My family argues all the time. How do I stay calm?

steps: Memorize *a'udhu billahi minash-shaytanir-rajim* as your anger reset
Next time you feel heat rising, say it and stay quiet for ten seconds
screens.optional_extra: Is there someone you snapped at recently? Apologize today, briefly and sincerely.

screens.text: Real strength is controlling yourself when angry. Seek refuge in Allah, sit down, stay quiet, and come back to the problem calm.
Every time you hold your tongue in anger, you're getting stronger.

check.prompt: Who did the Prophet ﷺ call truly strong?

options.text: The one who controls themselves when angry
options.feedback: Right [Bukhari 6114]. Self-control is the real strength.

options.text: The one who wins every argument
options.feedback: Not quite. The strong one controls themselves when angry [Bukhari 6114].

check.prompt: You're standing and getting angry. What did the Prophet ﷺ advise?

options.text: Sit down, and if it doesn't pass, lie down
options.feedback: Right [Abu Dawud 4782]. Changing position helps the anger cool.

options.text: Say what you feel right away so it doesn't build up
options.feedback: Not quite. He advised changing position and staying quiet first [Abu Dawud 4782; Bukhari 6018].

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Asked for advice, the Prophet ﷺ told a man not to get angry, and repeated it each time he asked again [Bukhari 6116].
- The strong one controls himself in anger [Bukhari 6114].
- Seeking refuge in Allah from Satan removes anger [Bukhari 6115]; if standing, sit; if it persists, lie down [Abu Dawud 4782, sahih per al-Albani].
- Say good or stay silent [Bukhari 6018]. Restrain anger and pardon [Q 3:134]; repel bad with better [Q 41:34].
- Anger has a balanced place: rage is a vice, but appropriate anger at injustice can be right [Being Muslim, Spiritual Refinement].

**Likely questions**
- *"I can't let go of anger at someone at the masjid."* Validate; suggest du'a for the person, some distance, and talking to the mentor or imam if it involves real mistreatment. Pardon is rewarded but not forced.
- *"How do I apologize?"* Short, specific, no "but": "I'm sorry I snapped. That wasn't fair to you."
- *"Anger at injustice?"* It can be right; channel it into just action and calm words, not cruelty.
- *"Family argues constantly."* Use the tools, step away, pick calm times for real talks; link Days 14, 35 and 65.
- *"Does anger break wudu?"* No. (Hanafi: loud laughter in salah breaks wudu, but anger and shouting don't.) Don't overload.

**Escalate:** conflict with masjid staff or leaders, or mistreatment at the masjid (mentor/imam). **Safety first:** if anyone's anger, at home or elsewhere, involves threats, violence or fear, follow the safety rule (crisis resources, consent-based alert). If the convert fears their own anger could hurt someone, respond with care and point to professional help.

**Don't**
- Don't tell a convert to "just be patient" with abuse.
- Don't play or describe imams or scholars as the angry party in examples; keep characters as ordinary community members (Spec §6.2 rule 13).
